Synopsis:
    IG Metall is threatening maximum resistance ahead of a critical VW supervisory board meeting (Friday) where three rival restructuring proposals will be voted on. VW management warns of a €1.5bn/year cost disadvantage if excess capacity at Hanover, Emden, Neckarsulm and Zwickau is not cut. The stand-off risks escalation to an extraordinary shareholder meeting. The dispute centers on potential plant closures and ~50,000 layoffs, revisiting a restructuring package agreed less than two years ago.

Q01. Is the content's main message about EU energy, EU commodities, German power market prices, German energy economics?
Relevance: NO — The article is about VW's industrial restructuring and labour relations, not energy markets or commodities.

Q02. Is the content confirming already known information or reporting very new/uncertain risks?
Risk score: 35 — The VW-IG Metall dispute is an ongoing, publicly known conflict. The escalation ahead of the Friday board vote adds some new near-term uncertainty, but the broad contours of the restructuring battle are not surprising given the context established over prior months.

Q03. Is the content explicit about bullish impact on the German power futures market?
Explicit: NO
Impact score: 5 — No explicit bullish signal for German power. Marginally, large-scale plant closures if realised could reduce industrial power demand, but this is indirect and speculative.

Q04. Is the content explicit about bearish impact on the German power futures market?
Explicit: NO
Impact score: 10 — If VW plant closures proceed (Hanover, Emden, Neckarsulm, Zwickau), the reduction in heavy industrial electricity consumption could exert mild bearish pressure on German baseload demand, but the article makes no explicit connection to power markets, and any such effect would be modest and long-dated.
